chunks.text: 3 Method Circuit Fine-Tuning (CFT) consists of two phases: (1) distribution-aware circuit discovery (Sec. 3.1 ), which identifies and selects a target-distribution responsive circuit, and (2) sparse circuit adaptation (Sec. 3.2 ), which fine-tunes only the discovered modules. Preliminaries: EAP-IG. The goal of Edge Attribution Patching with Integrated Gradients (EAP-IG) (Hanna et al. 2024 ) is to approximate the effect of activation patching of module m m via path-integrated gradients (Sundararajan et al. 2017 ) : ϕ m ​ ( x ) ≈ ( a m ​ ( x ′ ) − a m ​ ( x ) ) ⋅ 1 S ​ ∑ s = 1 S ∂ F ​ ( x ′ + s S ​ ( x − x ′ ) ) ∂ a m , \phi_{m}(x)\approx\bigl(a_{m}(x^{\prime})-a_{m}(x)\bigr)\cdot\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\frac{\partial F\!\left(x^{\prime}+\tfrac{s}{S}(x-x^{\prime})\right)}{\partial a_{m}}\,, (1) where x ′ x^{\prime} is a baseline image, F F is a scalar output ( e.g. , cross-entropy), and each of the S S steps costs one forward-backward pass ( 2 ​ S 2S passes total). Module granularity. We define the computational graph at the level of functional units within each Transformer block ℓ ∈ { 1 , … , L } \ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\} . Rather than individual weight matrices, each node in the graph represents either an individual attention head or the complete MLP unit. Specifically, each block ℓ \ell contains H H attention head nodes { h 1 ℓ , … , h H ℓ } \{h_{1}^{\ell},\ldots,h_{H}^{\ell}\} and one MLP node m ℓ m^{\ell} . For ViT-B/16 ( L = 12 , H = 12 L=12,H=12 ), this configuration yields 156 candidate nodes ( 13 13 nodes per layer). Circuit discovery algorithm. We evaluate several circuit discovery methods, and select EAP-IG (See Supp.). 3.1 Phase 1: Distribution-Aware Circuit Discovery The goal is to identify which circuits are most responsive to the target input distribution before any training occurs. Variance decomposition: why a single near-zero probe suffices.

We replace the pretrained classification head with a probe head W probe ∈ ℝ d × C W_{\text{probe}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times C} initialized from 𝒩 ​ ( 0 , σ 2 ) \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) with σ = 10 − 5 \sigma=10^{-5} . The purpose is to reduce the influence of arbitrary class preferences induced by a randomly initialized head, so that the attribution scores more reliably reflect the backbone’s response to the target distribution. The total variance of the importance score ϕ m \phi_{m} can be decomposed by the law of total variance: Var ​ [ ϕ m ] = \displaystyle\mathrm{Var}[\phi_{m}]={} Var W probe ​ [ 𝔼 ℬ ​ [ ϕ m ∣ W probe ] ] ⏟ (i) probe-initialization variance \displaystyle\underbrace{\mathrm{Var}_{W_{\mathrm{probe}}}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{B}}\!\left[\phi_{m}\mid W_{\mathrm{probe}}\right]\right]}_{\text{(i) probe-initialization variance}} (2) + 𝔼 W probe ​ [ Var ℬ ​ [ ϕ m ∣ W probe ] ] ⏟ (ii) calibration-sample variance . \displaystyle+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{W_{\mathrm{probe}}}\!\left[\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{B}}\!\left[\phi_{m}\mid W_{\mathrm{probe}}\right]\right]}_{\text{(ii) calibration-sample variance}}. Term (i) measures how much the importance scores vary across random probe heads, while term (ii) measures variance induced by the finite calibration batch. With a standard-scale head ( e.g. , Kaiming initialization, σ ≈ 0.05 \sigma\approx 0.05 ), and assuming approximately unit-variance features, each logit z c = W probe , c ⊤ ​ h z_{c}=W_{\text{probe},c}^{\top}h has standard deviation σ ​ d ≈ 1.4 \sigma\sqrt{d}\approx 1.4 for ViT-B/16 ( d = 768 d=768 ). Consequently, the softmax can exhibit strong random class preferences, causing different probe draws to produce different gradients and importance rankings. With near-zero initialization ( σ = 10 − 5 \sigma=10^{-5} ), the logit standard deviation drops to approximately 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} and the softmax remains close to uniform, p ^ c ≈ 1 / C \hat{p}_{c}\approx 1/C .

The output-gradient term therefore approaches ( 1 / C − y ) (1/C-y) . Near-zero initialization suppresses arbitrary high-confidence predictions and substantially reduces dependence on the particular probe draw and its influence on EAP-IG circuit discovery and improves the selection (Table 1 ). A natural question is whether ensembling multiple random probe heads—running discovery R R times with independent draws of W probe W_{\text{probe}} and averaging the resulting importance scores—would improve the recovered subgraph. As shown in Table 2 , increasing the ensemble size from R = 1 R=1 to R = 10 R=10 with near-zero initialization changes downstream accuracy by at most 0.1 0.1 percentage points and we therefore use R = 1 R=1 . For each module m m , we compute the aggregated importance: Φ m = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N | ϕ m ​ ( x i ) | . \Phi_{m}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|\phi_{m}(x_{i})|\,.

Circuit selection (parameter-budgeted node set). Let ℳ \mathcal{M} be the set of candidate nodes (attention heads and MLP blocks) and let Φ m \Phi_{m} denote the aggregated EAP-IG importance of node m m computed over the calibration set (Eq. 3 ). In our implementation, we normalize node scores by parameter count to avoid systematically favoring large modules: Φ ~ m = Φ m | θ m | , \tilde{\Phi}_{m}=\frac{\Phi_{m}}{|\theta_{m}|}, (4) where | θ m | |\theta_{m}| is the number of parameters in node m m (See Supp.). We then sort nodes by Φ ~ m \tilde{\Phi}_{m} in descending order to obtain a ranked list. Rather than selecting the top- k % k\% nodes by a score percentile threshold, we define the circuit as the set of nodes whose cumulative parameter count fits a target parameter budget . Let P total P_{\text{total}} be the total number of backbone parameters and let k k be the desired tunable fraction. The budget is B = ⌊ k ⋅ P total ⌋ . B=\left\lfloor k\cdot P_{\text{total}}\right\rfloor. (5) We construct the circuit 𝒯 ⊆ ℳ \mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{M} using a two-stage greedy procedure: (1) select the highest-ranked from each layer (when feasible under budget) to ensure full layer coverage, then (2) fill the remaining budget by adding the next highest-ranked nodes until the budget is exhausted: 𝒯 = GreedyBudgetSelect ​ ( { ( m , Φ ~ m ) } m ∈ ℳ , { | θ m | } m ∈ ℳ , B ) . \mathcal{T}\;=\;\textsc{GreedyBudgetSelect}\!\left(\{(m,\tilde{\Phi}_{m})\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}},\{|\theta_{m}|\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}},B\right). (6) Finally, we define the binary mask M ∈ { 0 , 1 } | ℳ | M\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{M}|} by membership: M m = 𝟙 ​ [ m ∈ 𝒯 ] . M_{m}=\mathds{1}[m\in\mathcal{T}]. (7) This mask specifies the circuit for the target distribution and determines which nodes are updated during Phase 2.

Circuits are task-specific (no universal circuit). Figure 1 shows that circuits vary substantially across VTAB-1k tasks on Swin-V2-B. Out of 400 candidate nodes, no node appears in all 19 circuits. The frequency distribution is heavy-tailed: 28 nodes appear in only 1–2 tasks, while only 6 appear in ≥ \geq 12, forming shared bottlenecks split between late-stage MLPs and attention heads. Pairwise circuit overlap is well above the ∼ 15 % {\sim}15\% expected under random selection at matched budget, and is consistently higher within VTAB groups (Natural/Specialized/Structured) than across them. This indicates that CFT discovers task-conditioned computational subgraphs rather than a fixed global ranking, motivating discovery to be performed per task rather than reusing a single mask. EAP-IG with S S integration steps on N N samples requires 2 ​ S ​ N 2SN forward-backward passes. With S = 12 S{=}12 and N = 32 N{=}32 , this equals 768 passes.

Relative to one training epoch of size | 𝒟 | |\mathcal{D}| : Cost disc = 2 ​ S ​ N | 𝒟 | ​ epochs. \text{Cost}_{\text{disc}}=\frac{2SN}{|\mathcal{D}|}\text{ epochs.} (8) On VTAB-1k ( | 𝒟 | = 1 , 000 |\mathcal{D}|{=}1{,}000 ), this is ≈ \approx 0.8 epochs. On CIFAR-100 ( | 𝒟 | = 50 , 000 |\mathcal{D}|{=}50{,}000 ), it drops to ≈ \approx 0.015 epochs. On ImageNet ( | 𝒟 | = 1.28 ​ M |\mathcal{D}|{=}1.28\text{M} ), it is < < 0.001 epochs. The cost is small relative to training and amortizes rapidly on larger datasets. All compute figures in Sec. 4 include discovery cost. Training cost: FLOPs analysis. Let ℱ fwd \mathcal{F}_{\text{fwd}} denote the FLOPs of a forward pass through the full backbone. The backward pass can be decomposed into two components: (i) gradients with respect to intermediate activations and (ii) gradients with respect to model weights: ℱ bwd = ℱ bwd,act + ℱ bwd,w . \mathcal{F}_{\text{bwd}}=\mathcal{F}_{\text{bwd,act}}+\mathcal{F}_{\text{bwd,w}}. (9) In deep networks, backward computation is typically about twice the cost of the forward pass. For clarity and generality, we assume that these two components contribute equally to the backward cost, and that each is comparable to the forward cost: ℱ bwd,act ≈ ℱ bwd,w ≈ ℱ fwd . \mathcal{F}_{\text{bwd,act}}\approx\mathcal{F}_{\text{bwd,w}}\approx\mathcal{F}_{\text{fwd}}. (10) Thus a standard training step costs ℱ step ≈ ℱ fwd + ℱ bwd,act + ℱ bwd,w ≈ 3 ​ ℱ fwd . \mathcal{F}_{\text{step}}\approx\mathcal{F}_{\text{fwd}}+\mathcal{F}_{\text{bwd,act}}+\mathcal{F}_{\text{bwd,w}}\approx 3\mathcal{F}_{\text{fwd}}. (11) For fine-tuning methods that update only a fraction of the parameters, we consider a conservative (worst-case for CFT only) bound in which the full activation-gradient graph remains active ( i.e. , ℱ bwd,act = 1 \mathcal{F}_{\text{bwd,act}}=1 ).

In this case, only the weight-gradient term scales with the fraction of updated parameters α \alpha : ℱ step ​ ( α ) ≈ ℱ fwd + ℱ bwd,act + α ​ ℱ bwd,w ≈ ( 2 + α ) ​ ℱ fwd , \mathcal{F}_{\text{step}}(\alpha)\approx\mathcal{F}_{\text{fwd}}+\mathcal{F}_{\text{bwd,act}}+\alpha\,\mathcal{F}_{\text{bwd,w}}\approx(2+\alpha)\,\mathcal{F}_{\text{fwd}}, (12) where α \alpha ( e.g. , 0.03 0.03 vs. 0.15 0.15 ) is the fraction of parameters for which weight gradients are computed and updated during training. Inference cost and deployment. CFT modifies only the values of existing weight tensors. The architecture, tensor shapes, sequence length, and computational graph are identical to the original ViT. This guarantees: (1) 1 × 1\times inference latency : no additional tokens (VPT), no extra layers (AdaptFormer), no merge step (SSF/SPT at deployment); (2) full kernel compatibility : FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022 ) , xFormers, TensorRT, and ONNX export work without modification; and (3) drop-in deployment : the adapted model is a single .pth file loadable by any standard ViT implementation. The supplementary shows accuracy varies little across this range. 4.2 Results on VTAB-1k We evaluate three questions. First, how much accuracy does each method yield per unit of compute? This is our main result. Second, does building each baseline a recipe for a short schedule close the gap? Third, does an accuracy gap remain under very high compute? CFT reaches high accuracy with far less compute (Fig. 2 ). We run all methods in one implementation on the same hardware and count cumulative training FLOPs (forward and backward) and wall-clock time.

For every baseline we tune the learning rate over five values around its published default, { η def × 10 ± 1 , η def × 10 ± 1 / 2 , η def } \{\eta_{\text{def}}\times 10^{\pm 1},\eta_{\text{def}}\times 10^{\pm 1/2},\eta_{\text{def}}\} , and pick the best one on a held-out validation split. CFT uses a single default learning rate, and its compute numbers include the cost of circuit discovery. Figure 2 plots the result. Both panels show the same runs: the y-axis is mean accuracy over the 19 tasks, and each point is a per-epoch checkpoint. The left panel prices each checkpoint in training FLOPs; the right panel prices it in wall-clock time, which also captures overhead that FLOP counts miss. Three things follow. First, CFT is the highest curve across the low-compute range in both panels, and it reaches 72.4 accuracy within 1,351 TFLOPs and 7.6 minutes, in 20.4 epochs on average. Second, the baselines converge slowly: each needs 44–96 epochs, which is 2.3 2.3 – 6.6 × 6.6\times more FLOPs and 2.9 2.9 – 16.2 × 16.2\times more wall-clock time, to reach its own peak. The cost per epoch is similar across methods, so the whole gap comes from convergence speed. Third, the two panels do not agree on the ranking of the baselines: Pro-VPT, for example, is far worse in wall-clock time than in FLOPs, and Full Fine-Tuning reaches its own peak with fewer FLOPs than SPT or GPS. A natural question is whether the baselines are slow only because their recipes were written for long runs.

We therefore give each baseline a recipe built for the specific budget it is given, training a separate run per method per budget: the cosine schedule is annealed over that budget rather than over the published horizon, the warmup from the published recipe is kept and scaled to the budget, and the learning rate is retuned over the five values used in Figure 2 and selected on a held-out validation split. This setting is challenging and far from the ImageNet distribution the backbones were pretrained on: the dataset is small and class-imbalanced, and the images are high-resolution grayscale mammograms. Every method trains for the same 5 epochs, and every learning rate is chosen with the validation protocol of Sec. 4.1 . We test three backbones and report them in two tables, because the available baselines differ by architecture. Table 7 covers the standard ViT-B/16 and compares against PEFT methods built for plain ViTs (SSF, SPT, GPS, Pro-VPT). Table 8 covers the self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-B/14 (Oquab et al. 2024 ) and Swin Transformer (Swin-v2-B) (Liu et al. 2022 ) . We apply the same two baselines so that both blocks of Table 8 are directly comparable. This is a fixed-budget comparison rather than a converged one: it asks which method reaches the highest accuracy within a short schedule under domain shift, and does not establish which method is strongest given unlimited compute. Under this protocol CFT attains the highest accuracy on all three backbones. On ViT-B/16 its AUC (0.768) falls within the seed variation of the strongest baseline (SPT), so we read the two as comparable in ranking quality while CFT leads at the operating threshold. Stability. The standard deviation of accuracy is ± \pm 0.57 over 3 random seeds, ± \pm 0.013 for AUC. 4.4 Domain Shift 2: Vision-Language Model As a feasibility study, we apply CFT to Gemma-3-4B-IT on CUB-200 (Table 9 ). With a 5-epoch budget, CFT reaches 71.3% top-1 accuracy by training only the discovered circuit, which is 17 % 17\% of the backbone parameters. It outperforms both LoRA, which updates a far smaller fraction ( ∼ 0.5 % {\sim}0.5\% ), and full fine-tuning.

This is a claim about placement , not parameter efficiency. At a fixed short budget, concentrating updates on attribution-selected modules outperforms distributing low-rank updates uniformly across layers, and the remaining 83% of parameters updated by full fine-tuning yield no benefit within this budget. The supplementary shows accuracy varies little across this range. 4.2 Results on VTAB-1k We evaluate three questions. First, how much accuracy does each method yield per unit of compute? This is our main result. Second, does building each baseline a recipe for a short schedule close the gap? Third, does an accuracy gap remain under very high compute? CFT reaches high accuracy with far less compute (Fig. 2 ). We run all methods in one implementation on the same hardware and count cumulative training FLOPs (forward and backward) and wall-clock time. For every baseline we tune the learning rate over five values around its published default, { η def × 10 ± 1 , η def × 10 ± 1 / 2 , η def } \{\eta_{\text{def}}\times 10^{\pm 1},\eta_{\text{def}}\times 10^{\pm 1/2},\eta_{\text{def}}\} , and pick the best one on a held-out validation split. CFT uses a single default learning rate, and its compute numbers include the cost of circuit discovery. Figure 2 plots the result. Both panels show the same runs: the y-axis is mean accuracy over the 19 tasks, and each point is a per-epoch checkpoint. The left panel prices each checkpoint in training FLOPs; the right panel prices it in wall-clock time, which also captures overhead that FLOP counts miss. Three things follow. First, CFT is the highest curve across the low-compute range in both panels, and it reaches 72.4 accuracy within 1,351 TFLOPs and 7.6 minutes, in 20.4 epochs on average. Second, the baselines converge slowly: each needs 44–96 epochs, which is 2.3 2.3 – 6.6 × 6.6\times more FLOPs and 2.9 2.9 – 16.2 × 16.2\times more wall-clock time, to reach its own peak. The cost per epoch is similar across methods, so the whole gap comes from convergence speed.

Third, the two panels do not agree on the ranking of the baselines: Pro-VPT, for example, is far worse in wall-clock time than in FLOPs, and Full Fine-Tuning reaches its own peak with fewer FLOPs than SPT or GPS. With a 5-epoch budget, CFT reaches 71.3% top-1 accuracy by training only the discovered circuit, which is 17 % 17\% of the backbone parameters. It outperforms both LoRA, which updates a far smaller fraction ( ∼ 0.5 % {\sim}0.5\% ), and full fine-tuning. This is a claim about placement , not parameter efficiency. At a fixed short budget, concentrating updates on attribution-selected modules outperforms distributing low-rank updates uniformly across layers, and the remaining 83% of parameters updated by full fine-tuning yield no benefit within this budget. Across VTAB-1k, a mammography benchmark, and four backbones, CFT reaches accuracy within 0.7 0.7 points of the strongest baseline at 2.3 2.3 – 6.6 × 6.6\times fewer training FLOPs and up to 16 × 16\times less wall-clock time, with no learning-rate warmup and no added parameters.
